title: The attendance policy that backfired
author: Jayme Dyer
summary: Biology professor Jayme Dyer describes trying to replicate a published finding -- Cullen and Oppenheimer's (2024) Carnegie Mellon study showing that an opt-in attendance policy (versus a mandatory one) improved attendance because the act of opting in functioned as a pre-commitment device -- in her own community college classroom, and reports that it did not work. Her "Attendance Challenge" (a 3% grade bonus/penalty tied to opting in) produced no meaningful improvement in attendance when compared against a matched control section that ran with no attendance policy at all the following semester. Worse, closer inspection of the data suggested the policy may have actively harmed her most vulnerable students: three students who accumulated more than nine absences had all opted in to the challenge, versus just one in the no-policy control section, raising the possibility that once a student crossed the three-absence penalty threshold they gave up rather than being motivated to recover. Dyer is explicit that her sample is too small to prove causation, but she draws a clear practical lesson: this is the second time she has found that grading for attendance disproportionately penalizes students who are already struggling. She closes by preserving the more general insight behind the original study -- that increasing students' sense of autonomy can genuinely boost motivation -- while questioning whether an attendance policy tied to grades is an equitable way to deliver it.
points: Dyer's design choice matters as much as her result: she compared her opt-in section against a no-policy control section, whereas the original study compared opt-in against mandatory-with-the-same-penalty -- a methodological distinction she flags explicitly as the likely source of her divergent finding.

Her most consequential data point is not the null overall result but the tail: three high-absence students in the opt-in section (versus one in the control) all had opted in, suggesting the policy may concentrate harm on students who were already struggling rather than motivating them.

She names a specific psychological mechanism worth watching for in any threshold-based grading policy: once a student passes the point where the penalty is already "locked in," they may have less incentive to keep attending, not more.

Despite a null/negative result for her own implementation, she doesn't reject the underlying theory (autonomy as a motivator) -- she reframes the open question as one of equitable delivery mechanism, not of whether autonomy matters.
quotes: Cullen and Oppenheimer found that attendance was higher in the Opt-In sections than in the Mandatory sections, especially later in the semester. They argued that the difference in attendance is likely due to students' sense of autonomy: Making the choice to opt in to the attendance policy acted as a pre-commitment device, which motivated students to attend class.
However, by the end of that semester, it didn't feel like there was a dramatic improvement in attendance or tardiness. Now, I'm a scientist. I aim to make conclusions based on data, not feelings.
Because it felt unfair to my most vulnerable students, I quit using the Attendance Policy and didn't offer it in Spring 2026.
In my spring 2026 section, one student had more than 9 absences, but in my Fall 2025 section, three students had more than 9 absences and all three of them had opted in to the Attendance Challenge.

First, it didn't appear to improve attendance. Second, it disproportionately penalized students who were already struggling. The average final course grade of the opt-in students with more than 3 absences was 71% before the 3% penalty.
Significant psychological research has shown that increasing one's sense of autonomy can increase motivation and achievement. In what other ways can we offer students more autonomy in our courses?
